report.summary: Reviewed daedalus/lanes/checks.py chunk 1 of 2: baseline guard functions, dataclasses, AST helpers; all docstring claims checked against visible code, verdicts mostly KEPT with a few UNCHECKABLE.
risks: not_substituted | high | The docstring claims it catches 'complete, valid, well-formed' substitutions, but the code's toplevel_defs returns None on parse failure; then not_substituted returns '' and leaves the substitution to other guards. The claim 'a substitution keeps none of them' is only true when the substituted file parses. The docstring's example substituted a valid test file, so it parses, but a substitution of a non-Python or unparsable file would slip. What would settle it: a test with a non-parsing substituted file.

parses | medium | The fallback ast.parse after toplevel_defs returns None is nearly unreachable: toplevel_defs already returns None on SyntaxError, ValueError, RecursionError, so the only way to reach the except clauses is if ast.parse behaves differently between calls (e.g., due to mutation of the string). The 'pragma: no cover' comment acknowledges this, but the dead branch could mislead future maintainers. What would settle it: a test that forces the second parse to fail while the first succeeds.

CheckPolicy | low | The docstring says 'Everything here is a claim about a MODEL', but first_party_roots is a repository fact, not a model claim. This is a documentation inconsistency that could mislead policy tuning. What would settle it: review of the policy's intent in docs.

no_elision | low | The check lowercases the entire proposed and original text, which could cause a false positive if a marker word appears inside a string literal or comment in the original but not in the proposed. The docstring says 'Only NEW markers count', but the implementation does not distinguish code vs. prose. What would settle it: a test with a marker inside a string.

not_truncated | low | The check compares raw character lengths, not semantic content. A rewrite that removes a large comment block could be flagged as truncation even if all code is preserved. The docstring says 'the model returned part of the file', but the check only measures size. What would settle it: a test with a large comment removal.

toplevel_defs | low | The function only counts top-level defs/classes, not imports or assignments. A substitution that keeps the same function names but changes all imports would pass not_substituted. The docstring says 'does the result still contain the thing that was sent?', but it only checks names. What would settle it: a test with a substitution that keeps names but changes imports.

uncheckable claims | low | Several claims reference behavior outside this chunk (run_checks, _exports, imports_resolve, no_elision tests). These are marked UNCHECKABLE and need verification in the rest of the file or tests. What would settle it: review of the remaining chunks and test files.
todos: Verify not_substituted's behavior on non-parsing substitutions in chunk 2 or tests.
Check if parses's second ast.parse branch is reachable in practice.
Review CheckPolicy docstring for first_party_roots classification.
Confirm no_elision's case-insensitive marker matching is intended.
Check not_truncated's size-only heuristic against real truncation cases.
Verify the claims marked UNCHECKABLE in the rest of the file.

handoff.purpose: Baseline guard functions and shared AST helpers for write lanes.

symbols.name: WriteAttempt
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass bundling rel, proposed, repo_root, original, creating; is_python property checks .py suffix.

symbols.name: CheckPolicy
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass with policy dials: elision_markers, min_size_ratio, min_symbol_survival, min_symbols_to_judge, first_party_roots, max_named_imports.

symbols.name: BASELINE_POLICY
symbols.note: Default CheckPolicy instance with all defaults.

symbols.name: toplevel_defs
symbols.note: Parses source, returns frozenset of top-level def/class names, or None on parse failure.

symbols.name: _module_path
symbols.note: Resolves dotted module to .py file, __init__.py, or namespace directory with at least one .py; returns None if not found.

symbols.name: _exports
symbols.note: Parses a module file and returns (top-level names, opaque flag) for star-imports or __getattr__.

symbols.name: parses
symbols.note: Refuses if proposed Python does not parse; skips if not Python, or if original already unparsable and not creating.

symbols.name: not_truncated
symbols.note: Refuses if proposed length is below min_size_ratio of original length; skips on creating or empty original.

symbols.name: no_elision
symbols.note: Refuses if a policy elision marker appears in proposed but not in original (case-insensitive).

symbols.name: not_substituted
symbols.note: Refuses if top-level symbol survival is below policy thresholds; skips if not Python, creating, or original unparsable.

claims.text: A check returns "" to pass and a human-readable reason to refuse; a check that RAISES is treated as a refusal, because a guard that cannot answer must not be read as consent.
claims.why: The chunk defines the checks but does not show the runner (run_checks) that would catch exceptions. The claim about RAISES is not verifiable here.

claims.text: Deviation from the shape sketched in docs/HANDOFF_2026-07-30_NIGHT.md, which proposed ``Check = (rel, original, proposed, repo_root, policy) -> str``: the first four arguments are bundled into :class:`WriteAttempt`.
claims.why: The referenced doc file is not provided; the claim about the deviation is a historical note, not checkable against code.

claims.text: Two of the baseline checks need a fifth fact (is this file being CREATED, so that there is no original to compare against), and a positional signature that has to grow every time a check needs one more fact is a signature every lane has to be edited to match. The dataclass grows instead.
claims.why: WriteAttempt includes a creating field and the checks (not_truncated, not_substituted, parses) use it. The dataclass indeed grows instead of the signature.

claims.text: ``original`` is the exact current text, or "" when ``creating``. Keeping the two facts separate rather than inferring "creating" from an empty original matters: a lane that truncates a real file to nothing must not be able to present that as a creation and skip the guards that only run on edits.
claims.why: WriteAttempt has both original and creating fields with defaults; not_truncated and not_substituted skip when creating, so a truncated file with creating=False would be caught by not_truncated.

claims.text: The per-lane dials. Everything here is a claim about a MODEL, not about the repository -- which is exactly why it is a parameter and not a constant.
claims.why: The first_party_roots field is a claim about the repository (which roots belong to it), not about a model. The docstring overgeneralizes.

claims.text: Only refused when the marker is NEW, so a file that legitimately contains the phrase does not become unwritable.
claims.why: no_elision checks that the marker is in proposed but not in original, so pre-existing markers are not refused.

claims.text: Below this fraction of the original size, a "full rewrite" is a truncation.
claims.why: not_truncated uses this ratio to refuse when proposed length is below ratio * original length.

claims.text: Below this fraction of surviving top-level definitions, a "rewrite" is a different file rather than an edited one. 0.5 is deliberately permissive: a genuine refactor can rename or merge a lot, and refusing a real change costs twice -- the work is lost AND the task escalates to a paid lane. The failures this exists to catch were TOTAL substitutions (0% survival), so a loose threshold still stops them.
claims.why: The threshold is defined here, but the actual survival calculation is in not_substituted which is cut off at the end of the chunk. The claim about 0.5 being permissive is not verifiable without the full function.

claims.text: Below this many top-level definitions the survival ratio is noise -- losing one of two functions is an ordinary edit.
claims.why: The comment describes the policy intent, but the usage of min_symbols_to_judge is in the truncated part of not_substituted, so it cannot be checked here.

claims.text: A missing third-party package is an environment question and none of this gate's business; a missing first-party module is a file the model invented.
claims.why: The comment describes the policy's intent, but the actual import resolution logic is in imports_resolve, which is not in this chunk.

claims.text: How many unresolved imports to name in a refusal before summarising.
claims.why: The field is defined here, but the refusal message construction is in imports_resolve, not in this chunk.

claims.text: Top-level function and class names, or None if the text will not parse. Only the TOP level: a rewrite is free to reorganise nested helpers, and counting those would make ordinary refactors look like substitutions.
claims.why: The function parses the source and returns a frozenset of names from tree.body only, checking FunctionDef, AsyncFunctionDef, ClassDef. It returns None on SyntaxError, ValueError, RecursionError.

claims.text: A directory WITHOUT ``__init__.py`` still counts. Since Python 3.3 such a directory is an implicit namespace package (PEP 420) and imports perfectly well -- ``tools`` and ``tests`` in this repository are exactly that, and both import fine while reporting ``__file__ is None``.
claims.why: The function checks a directory without __init__.py and returns it if it contains at least one .py file.

claims.text: MEASURED 2026-07-30: without this branch the gate reported "module 'tools' does not exist" for `tests/test_iron_plan_guard.py`, a real committed file that imports it, and `test_no_false_positives_across_the_real_tree` failed with its own message -- "this gate must never refuse real repo code". Any lane writing a module that imports `tools` or `tests` would have been refused for importing something that is demonstrably there.
claims.why: The claim references a specific test and historical failure; no test file is provided in this chunk, so it cannot be verified.

claims.text: This does not loosen the guard. The invented imports it exists to catch -- ``daedalus.linting``, ``daedalus.wiki_vault`` -- name directories that do not exist either, so they are still refused. A directory is required to contain at least one ``.py`` file, so an empty or data-only folder cannot launder an import that would fail at runtime.
claims.why: The function only returns a namespace directory if it contains at least one .py file, so empty or data-only directories are not returned. The examples of invented imports are not directly checkable, but the behavior is as described.

claims.text: The returned directory is deliberately not a readable module: :func:`_exports` fails closed on it (an OSError becomes ``opaque=True``), which is the honest answer, because what a namespace package provides is its submodules and no single file lists them.
claims.why: The claim references _exports's behavior, which is defined later in the chunk, but the specific failure mode (OSError becoming opaque=True) is in _exports, which is present. However, the claim that the returned directory causes an OSError is not directly testable without files. The _exports function does catch OSError and returns (frozenset(), True), so the behavior is consistent, but the claim about the specific directory causing OSError is uncheckable without actual paths.

claims.text: ``opaque`` means static reading is not authoritative for this module -- it star-imports or defines a module-level ``__getattr__``, either of which can legitimately provide a name no reader can see.
claims.why: The function sets opaque=True when it sees a star import or a top-level __getattr__ definition. It also returns opaque=True on any parse error, which is consistent with 'not authoritative'.

claims.text: A Python file that will not parse is not an improvement. Runs on CREATED files too, which is where the hole was: an edit that stops parsing was caught by :func:`not_substituted` as a side effect, but a brand-new module that does not parse had nothing looking at it -- the imports check returns early on a parse failure, calling it "a different guard's business". This is that guard.
claims.why: parses runs on created files (does not skip when creating). It refuses when proposed does not parse. The claim about imports check returning early is not checkable here, but the guard's behavior is as described.

claims.text: The classic full-rewrite failure: the model returned part of the file.
claims.why: not_truncated refuses when proposed length is below the ratio, which is the classic truncation heuristic.

claims.text: The model admitting, in prose, that it dropped code. Only NEW markers count. A file that already contained the phrase would otherwise become permanently unwritable by this lane.
claims.why: no_elision only refuses when the marker is in proposed but not in original, so pre-existing markers are not refused.

claims.text: Why this "rewrite" looks like the WRONG FILE, or "" if it looks fine. MEASURED 2026-07-30, and the reason this exists. A change request naming two files is sent once per file; asked to rewrite ``daedalus/shift.py`` the model returned the contents of ``tests/test_shift.py``. The module was destroyed and the run reported ``status: done``. Three of five multi-file writes failed exactly this way. None of the other guards can see it. Truncation compares SIZE, and a substituted file is a perfectly normal size -- the test module was in fact larger than the module it replaced. Elision looks for a model admitting it omitted something, and nothing was omitted: a complete, valid, well-formed file arrived. It was simply the wrong one. So this asks the only question that separates the two cases: does the result still contain the thing that was sent? An edit keeps most of a file's top-level names; a substitution keeps none of them. Deliberately Python-only. The check needs a parser to be meaningful, and a guess about other languages would either fire on ordinary edits or provide false assurance for files it cannot actually read.
claims.why: The docstring describes the motivation and behavior, but the actual survival calculation is in the truncated part of the function. The claim that a substitution keeps none of the top-level names is not verifiable without the rest of the function, though the beginning shows it compares toplevel_defs of original and proposed.

claims.text: A check that CANNOT FAIL: an assertion comparing something with itself, a test whose fixture is derived from the thing under test, a branch no input reaches.
claims.why: The second ast.parse call after toplevel_defs returns None is nearly unreachable because toplevel_defs already returns None on the same exceptions. The only way to reach the except clauses is if the second parse fails while the first succeeded, which would require the string to change between calls. The 'pragma: no cover' comment confirms this is dead code in practice.

not_substituted's docstring claims it catches substitutions, but the code only compares top-level names; the rest of the function is cut off, so the survival calculation is unverified.
